blocks.text: A server can accept connections, create threads, and return correct answers while still lacking a safe shutdown path. topics.title: 21.1.1 Separating Networking from Application Logic
topics.summary: The request processor accepts a string view and returns a response string. It knows nothing about file descriptors, threads, ports, or clocks. blocks.text: The transport adapter receives a length-prefixed frame, invokes the processor, and sends the result. A syntax error is an ordinary application response, while an incomplete frame is a transport failure. Keeping these categories separate makes it possible to test malformed requests without opening sockets and to test the network contract without redesigning the arithmetic.

blocks.text: Separate the pure request processor from the transport adapter. The processor receives an owned or borrowed bounded request value and returns an owned response. It does not accept sockets, poll, launch threads, or modify process-wide configuration. This permits deterministic tests of syntax and arithmetic without requiring a live network. The transport layer remains responsible for framing, partial transfers, EOF classification, and connection ownership.

blocks.text: The example grammar is intentionally small: a command SUM followed by one to sixty-four bounded integers. Each token must parse completely; trailing junk is not accepted as a valid prefix. Numeric bounds make the accumulator’s arithmetic representable. Unknown commands, missing values, too many values, and invalid numeric tokens produce explicit application error responses rather than transport exceptions.

blocks.text: A framing error and an application rejection belong to different layers. A correctly framed payload containing an unknown command is still a complete transport message. An oversized declared length is rejected before allocating or parsing that payload. A peer that closes halfway through a header has not submitted a complete request at all. Preserve these distinctions in metrics and tests.

blocks.text: Keep platform-specific code behind a narrow boundary. Linux descriptor ownership, nonblocking flags, poll events, and MSG_NOSIGNAL belong in the native adapter. The pure grammar and bounded arithmetic can remain portable C++. This separation does not guarantee that the entire server compiles on Windows; it identifies which components would need another implementation and which tests can be reused.

topics.title: 21.1.2 Managing Client Connections
topics.summary: Each accepted descriptor has one owner. The acceptor moves it into the queue, a worker moves it out, and the worker’s local RAII wrapper closes it when processing ends. Queue insertion failure or exceptional unwinding also destroys the owned wrapper; no second component needs to guess who should close the connection.

Queue insertion failure or exceptional unwinding also destroys the owned wrapper; no second component needs to guess who should close the connection.

blocks.text: The shared Linux support implements four-byte big-endian length framing with a 4,096-byte payload ceiling. It handles partial transfers and suppresses SIGPIPE on sends. The fixture binds only to loopback and uses bounded waits. Those constraints reduce laboratory hazards but are not an authentication boundary against other local processes.
rich: The shared Linux support implements four-byte big-endian length framing with a 4,096-byte payload ceiling. It handles partial transfers and suppresses SIGPIPE on sends. The fixture binds only to loopback and uses bounded waits. Those constraints reduce laboratory hazards but are not an authentication boundary against other local processes.

blocks.text: A connection should have one clear owner at every stage: accepted by the listener, temporarily held by the acceptor, transferred into the queue if admitted, moved to a worker, and finally closed by that worker’s scope. A rejected queue insertion must release or return the connection according to the API contract. Copying descriptor integers across these stages obscures who is responsible for closing them.
rich: A connection should have one clear owner at every stage: accepted by the listener, temporarily held by the acceptor, transferred into the queue if admitted, moved to a worker, and finally closed by that worker’s scope. A rejected queue insertion must release or return the connection according to the API contract. Copying descriptor integers across these stages obscures who is responsible for closing them.

blocks.text: Bound admission before retaining unbounded work. A queue capacity limits queued items, while active workers and the acceptor can own additional descriptors. The extended server uses a nonblocking try-push policy: when the queue is full, the newly accepted connection is rejected and closed instead of blocking the acceptor indefinitely. This policy favors bounded retention and responsive stop checks over guaranteed admission of every arriving client.
rich: Bound admission before retaining unbounded work. A queue capacity limits queued items, while active workers and the acceptor can own additional descriptors. The extended server uses a nonblocking try-push policy: when the queue is full, the newly accepted connection is rejected and closed instead of blocking the acceptor indefinitely. This policy favors bounded retention and responsive stop checks over guaranteed admission of every arriving client.

blocks.text: Each accepted request also has a byte and time budget. The protocol caps payload size before allocation. An absolute deadline limits the allowed time for a complete framed read and response write in the extended implementation. The deadline is carried through partial progress, so a peer cannot indefinitely restart it by supplying one more byte. Ordinary OS scheduling still prevents this from being a hard real-time guarantee.
rich: Each accepted request also has a byte and time budget. The protocol caps payload size before allocation. The deadline is carried through partial progress, so a peer cannot indefinitely restart it by supplying one more byte. Ordinary OS scheduling still prevents this from being a hard real-time guarantee.

blocks.text: Connection cancellation should not depend on unsafely closing a descriptor from another thread while a worker is using it. The extended adapter uses nonblocking operations and bounded poll slices that recheck stop state. The owner closes the connection after leaving the operation. This preserves ownership and avoids assuming that a cross-thread close reliably interrupts every blocked call on every platform.

blocks.text: A listener’s stop path must be independent of receiving a final client. A fixed connection count is useful for a deterministic elementary fixture but unsuitable as the only shutdown mechanism for a long-running service. The extended server checks an explicit stop state while waiting for new connections and while workers process active ones, then closes the queue and joins before destroying shared state.

topics.title: 21.2.1 Implementing a Worker Pool
topics.summary: A fixed set of workers consumes accepted connections from a bounded queue. When the queue fills, the acceptor waits rather than allocating an unlimited number of pending tasks. The kernel’s listen backlog is another queue with a separate capacity and failure behavior; bounding one queue does not eliminate all overload states.

blocks.text: Closing the work queue wakes idle workers and prevents additional insertions. Accepted items are drained before workers exit. A guard declared after the worker container closes the queue before jthread destruction can join workers during exceptional startup. Per-connection failures are counted and isolated, while an acceptor failure is rethrown after orderly cleanup.

blocks.text: A worker pool separates task admission from execution. A fixed number of worker owners consume a bounded queue. This controls concurrency and avoids creating a new thread for every connection, but it adds queue and shutdown semantics that the one-thread-per-example model did not need. Define those semantics before choosing a container or thread-count default.

blocks.text: Queue closure and active cancellation can be combined deliberately. Closing prevents new admission and wakes idle workers. Workers can stop rather than drain every queued request when the documented shutdown policy chooses cancellation. Each queued owner must still be destroyed exactly once, and active owners remain alive until their operations observe stop or deadline and exit. The report should say whether pending work was completed or cancelled.

blocks.text: Startup must be exception-safe before the pool is fully populated. Create shared queue and stop state before workers, install the cleanup that can make blocked workers finish, and only then start additional threads. If worker creation fails partway through, close or cancel the queue, request stop where needed, and join already-started workers while all referenced state remains alive. This is a required architecture path, not a rare implementation detail to leave untested.

topics.title: 21.2.2 Measuring Throughput and Latency
topics.summary: Throughput counts completed work per unit of time; latency measures the delay experienced by a particular request. Report both with the workload definition, concurrency, message sizes, and error count. A server that rejects requests quickly can have excellent response timing without providing useful service.

paragraphs: Start with pure processor tests for valid sums, empty input, unknown command, malformed integer, too many values, and numeric bounds. Then run transport tests with fragmented headers, fragmented bodies, empty frames, oversized declarations, and truncated input. Keep the two test layers separate so a failure identifies the responsible contract.

Exercise the extended server’s independent stop path with no clients, an idle accepted client, and completed clients. Verify that the listener and worker owners are joined before shared state is destroyed. Use controlled synchronization for startup; do not assume a server is ready merely because a thread has been created.
